opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For inference, the biggest thing I prioritize is efficiency in moving data. Compute is no longer the hard part. With today's large models, especially at inference time and particularly during the decode phase of a language model, you're mostly limited by memory bandwidth and by how well you can keep the model's weights and the KV cache close to the compute. So the first question I ask is how to minimize data movement. The answer for me has been dataflow. You don't execute the model one kernel at a time, writing intermediate results back to off-chip memory between operations. You map the whole computation spatially onto the chip and stream data through it, so operators are fused and intermediate values stay on chip.

The second priority is the memory hierarchy itself. We've found that you need a tiered system: a large amount of on-chip SRAM for bandwidth, high-bandwidth memory for the active working set, and then a big pool of DDR capacity behind that. That last tier matters a lot for things like serving many models, or many experts in a mixture-of-experts model, on a single system. You can switch between models in milliseconds instead of needing a huge cluster of GPUs just to hold all the parameters.

Third, I care about programmability and flexibility. Models change incredibly quickly, and an architecture that's hard-wired for today's transformer may be obsolete in a year and a half. So the hardware has to be reconfigurable, and the software stack has to let you compile new model architectures onto it without hand-tuning every kernel.

Finally, it really comes down to the metrics users care about: tokens per second per user, time to first token, and overall throughput per watt and per dollar. Agentic workflows chain many model calls together, so latency compounds. If you can deliver fast inference efficiently, you enable a whole class of applications that just aren't practical otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response describes switching between models in milliseconds and serving many experts, but does not identify low-latency switching between collaborating agents as an architectural priority.

r002.rationale: It says agentic workflows chain many model calls, so latency compounds, and connects fast inference to making applications practical.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here.

When I think about architectures for inference, the first thing I prioritize is data movement, not compute. The arithmetic is almost the easy part. What really determines performance and energy efficiency is how far you have to move the weights and activations, and how many times you move them. Going out to DRAM is orders of magnitude more expensive than doing a multiply-accumulate, so the whole design question becomes: how do you keep data on chip, close to where it's used, and flowing through the computation rather than bouncing back and forth through a memory hierarchy?

That leads to the second priority, which is matching the architecture to the structure of the application. Inference workloads are really dataflow graphs. If you build a machine that executes that graph spatially, where one stage feeds the next directly, you avoid writing intermediate results back to memory at all. That's the core idea behind reconfigurable dataflow. Instead of a fixed instruction stream with caches guessing at your access pattern, you configure the hardware to look like the model, and the data just streams through.

Third is flexibility over time. Models change fast. Transformers, mixture of experts, long contexts, speculative decoding, agentic workloads with lots of small requests. If you bake too many assumptions into silicon, you're obsolete before you ship. So I want enough reconfigurability to adapt the datapath and the memory layout to a new model without a new chip.

And finally, you can't separate the hardware from the software stack. The compiler has to be able to see the whole graph and map it onto the fabric. If programmers have to hand-tune kernels, you've already lost. So I'd say the priorities are minimize data movement, exploit dataflow and spatial parallelism, stay flexible, and make sure the compiler can actually deliver all of that to the user.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data movement, dataflow, flexibility, and compiler support, but does not identify low-latency switching between collaborating agents as a priority.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that interactive reasoning with sequential language-model calls motivates fast inference.

astra-6.text:
I start with the workload: what computation are we trying to perform, and what does the application need in terms of latency and throughput? In inference, those requirements can lead to very different architectural choices. An interactive application needs a fast response, while a system processing a large batch may care more about total throughput.

Then I look closely at data movement. Having a lot of arithmetic capability doesn’t help if you can’t get the weights and activations to the compute units efficiently. So memory capacity, bandwidth, and opportunities to reuse data are central to the design, along with energy efficiency.

Finally, I prioritize programmability. Models evolve, and the architecture needs enough flexibility—and a good enough software stack—to run those changing workloads efficiently. The goal is useful application performance, rather than simply a high peak operations-per-second number.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data movement and application performance but does not identify low-latency switching between agents as a priority.

r002.rationale: It says interactive applications need fast responses, but does not connect that need to interactive reasoning with sequential language-model calls.

sol-6.1.text:
I prioritize efficiency, but I look at it at the system level. How quickly can you deliver a useful result, how much energy does it take, and how effectively are you using the hardware? For inference, moving the model’s weights and intermediate results can be as important as the arithmetic itself. So the architecture needs to keep data close to the computation and minimize unnecessary movement.

Then there’s the balance between latency and throughput. An interactive application needs a fast response, while a service handling many requests also needs high utilization. You want an architecture that supports both, with enough flexibility to accommodate changes in models. And the software is essential: the compiler and runtime have to translate that architectural potential into performance that developers can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response discusses latency, throughput, and utilization generally, but does not identify low-latency switching between collaborating agents.

r002.rationale: It mentions fast responses for interactive applications, but does not connect fast inference to interactive reasoning that involves sequential language-model calls.
